claims.source: iMyoblast muscle xenografts undergo fetal-to-adult MYH isoform switching demonstrating their plasticity to respond to maturation signals provided by the host adult muscle.
claims.evidence: The introduction states the observation of MYH isoform switching in xenografts.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts generated from FSHD1, LGMDR7, LGMDR9, and WWS patient iPSCs model the molecular pathologies of these diseases.
claims.source: Finally, we show that iMyoblasts generated from Facioscapulohumeral Muscular Dystrophy (FSHD) Type 1 (FSHD1), Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy (LGMD) R7 and R9 (formerly LGMD2G and 2I), and Walker Warburg Syndrome (WWS) patient iPSCs model the molecular pathologies of these diseases.
claims.evidence: The introduction states that disease iMyoblasts model disease pathologies.

claims.claim: A two-step protocol was developed to isolate iMyoblasts from cultures of Ctrl and patient iPSCs, using transgene-free iPSC myogenic induction in combination with reserve cell selection.
claims.source: We developed a two-step protocol to isolate iMyoblasts from cultures of Ctrl and patient iPSCs, using transgene-free iPSC myogenic induction in combination with reserve cell selection (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the protocol development and Figure 1A illustrates it.

claims.claim: Human iPSC lines for these studies were generated by reprogramming bMyoblasts and fibroblasts isolated from muscle biopsies of adult FSHD1 and Ctrl subjects.
claims.source: Human iPSC lines for these studies were generated by reprogramming bMyoblasts and fibroblasts isolated from muscle biopsies of adult FSHD1 and Ctrl subjects (Homma et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2012), or dermal fibroblasts from subjects with early onset FSHD1, LGMDR7, LGMDR9, and WWS (Kava et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the source of iPSC lines with citations.

claims.claim: The first step of the iMyoblast protocol was transgene-free iPSC myogenesis induction using commercially available reagents.
claims.source: The first step of the iMyoblast protocol was transgene-free iPSC myogenesis induction using commercially available reagents (Caron et al., 2016; Amsbio, Skeletal Muscle differentiation Kit) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the first step of the protocol with citation and figure reference.

claims.claim: The three-stage iPSC myogenesis protocol induces cultures of Ctrl and disease iPSCs to sequentially upregulate expression of muscle master regulators, PAX3 (S1 stage) and MYOD1 (S2 stage), and the muscle differentiation marker MYH8 (S3 Stage).
claims.source: This three-stage iPSC myogenesis protocol induces cultures of Ctrl and disease iPSCs to sequentially upregulate expression of muscle master regulators, PAX3 (S1 stage) and MYOD1 (S2 stage), and the muscle differentiation marker MYH8 (S3 Stage) (Caron et al., 2016), as assayed by qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the sequential upregulation of markers with qPCR data shown in a figure.

claims.claim: Ctrl and disease iPSC and ESC lines robustly upregulated expression of PAX3, MYOD1, and MYH8 on the order of 1000-fold during S1, S2, and S3 stages of myogenic induction.
claims.source: These studies established that Ctrl and disease iPSC and ESC lines robustly upregulated expression of PAX3, MYOD1, and MYH8 on the order of 1000-fold during S1, S2, and S3 stages of myogenic induction, validating the consistency and efficiency of the transgene-free induction protocol.
claims.evidence: The Results section quantifies the upregulation of markers during induction.

claims.claim: 90% of cells in S2 stage cultures were MYOD1+.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence (IF) assays showed that 90% of cells in S2 stage cultures were MYOD1+, and 80% of cells in S3 stage cultures were MF20+ and predominantly mononucleated iMyocytes (Figure 1A), similar to the first myogenic cells to differentiate in the embryo (Lee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence assays quantified the percentage of MYOD1+ cells in S2 cultures.

claims.claim: 80% of cells in S3 stage cultures were MF20+ and predominantly mononucleated iMyocytes.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence (IF) assays showed that 90% of cells in S2 stage cultures were MYOD1+, and 80% of cells in S3 stage cultures were MF20+ and predominantly mononucleated iMyocytes (Figure 1A), similar to the first myogenic cells to differentiate in the embryo (Lee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence assays quantified the percentage of MF20+ cells in S3 cultures.

claims.claim: S3 stage iMyocytes are similar to the first myogenic cells to differentiate in the embryo.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence (IF) assays showed that 90% of cells in S2 stage cultures were MYOD1+, and 80% of cells in S3 stage cultures were MF20+ and predominantly mononucleated iMyocytes (Figure 1A), similar to the first myogenic cells to differentiate in the embryo (Lee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The Results section compares S3 iMyocytes to embryonic myogenic cells with citation.

claims.claim: PAX7 expression was detected at 100-fold lower levels than PAX3 during S1 induction.
claims.source: PAX7 expression was detected at 100-fold lower levels than PAX3 during S1 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with earlier findings that PAX7+ cells are a minor cell population induced by transgene-free myogenesis protocols (Chal et al., 2015; van der Wal et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed lower PAX7 expression compared to PAX3.

claims.claim: PAX7+ cells are a minor cell population induced by transgene-free myogenesis protocols.
claims.source: PAX7 expression was detected at 100-fold lower levels than PAX3 during S1 induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with earlier findings that PAX7+ cells are a minor cell population induced by transgene-free myogenesis protocols (Chal et al., 2015; van der Wal et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The Results section cites earlier findings about PAX7+ cells in transgene-free protocols.

claims.claim: bMyoblasts and iMyoblasts expressed muscle master regulatory genes PAX3 and MYOD1 in growth factor-rich medium.
claims.source: In growth factor-rich medium, bMyoblasts and iMyoblasts expressed muscle master regulatory genes PAX3 and MYOD1 whereas adult bMyoblasts expressed PAX7 in addition to PAX3 and MYOD1 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed expression of PAX3 and MYOD1 in both cell types.

claims.claim: Adult bMyoblasts expressed PAX7 in addition to PAX3 and MYOD1.
claims.source: In growth factor-rich medium, bMyoblasts and iMyoblasts expressed muscle master regulatory genes PAX3 and MYOD1 whereas adult bMyoblasts expressed PAX7 in addition to PAX3 and MYOD1 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed expression of PAX7, PAX3, and MYOD1 in adult bMyoblasts.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts proliferated in myoblast growth medium with 12 hr cell doubling times.
claims.source: iMyoblasts proliferated in myoblast growth medium with 12 hr cell doubling times and could be expanded as primary lines for more than 12 passages (>30 population doublings) while cell-autonomously maintaining expression of PAX3 and MYOD1 and the commitment to differentiate in response to growth factor free medium, as assayed by expression of MYH8 and CKM (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The Results section states the cell doubling time for iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts could be expanded as primary lines for more than 12 passages (>30 population doublings) while cell-autonomously maintaining expression of PAX3 and MYOD1 and the commitment to differentiate.
claims.source: iMyoblasts proliferated in myoblast growth medium with 12 hr cell doubling times and could be expanded as primary lines for more than 12 passages (>30 population doublings) while cell-autonomously maintaining expression of PAX3 and MYOD1 and the commitment to differentiate in response to growth factor free medium, as assayed by expression of MYH8 and CKM (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the expansion capacity and maintenance of myogenic markers in iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: During their differentiation, iMyoblasts fused to form multinucleated iMyotubes.
claims.source: During their differentiation, iMyoblasts fused to form multinucleated iMyotubes (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence images showed multinucleated iMyotubes.

claims.claim: Proliferating FSHD1 and Ctrl iMyoblasts expressed cell surface markers typical of fetal and adult myogenic cells, including CD82, CD56, CD318, ERBB3, and NGFR.
claims.source: Proliferating FSHD1 and Ctrl iMyoblasts expressed cell surface markers typical of fetal and adult myogenic cells, including CD82 (Alexander et al., 2016; Pakula et al., 2019) as well as CD56, CD318 (Uezumi et al., 2016), ERBB3, and NGFR (Hicks et al., 2018; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Flow cytometry data showed expression of multiple cell surface markers.

claims.claim: FAC-sorted CD82+/CD56+ and CD82+/CD56− iMyoblasts both differentiated and fused to form MF20+ iMyotubes.
claims.source: FAC-sorted CD82+/CD56+ and CD82+/CD56− iMyoblasts both differentiated and fused to form MF20+ iMyotubes, validating the commitment of CD82+ iMyoblasts to differentiate (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Immunofluorescence of sorted cells showed differentiation capacity.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts retained their dual commitment to both differentiate and generate reserve cells that could be recovered by growth medium stimulation as MYOD1+ iMyoblasts (tMyoblasts) that can fuse and differentiate as MF20+ and MEF2C + iMyotubes.
claims.source: Finally, iMyoblasts retained their dual commitment to both differentiate and generate reserve cells that could be recovered by growth medium stimulation as MYOD1+ iMyoblasts (tMyoblasts) that can fuse and differentiate as MF20+ and MEF2C + iMyotubes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Reserve cell selection experiments showed the dual commitment of iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) was used to define the iMyoblast transcriptome and compare it to transcriptome signatures of adult muscle bMyoblasts, and S1 and S2 stage cells undergoing iPSC myogenic induction.
claims.source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) was used to define the iMyoblast transcriptome and compare it to transcriptome signatures of adult muscle bMyoblasts, and S1 and S2 stage cells undergoing iPSC myogenic induction.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the use of scRNA-Seq for transcriptome analysis.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts were generated by iPSC induction and reserve cell propagation from S3 cultures from iPSCs reprogrammed from parental CD56+ muscle biopsy cells of six subjects, including two classic FSHD1 subjects (15A and 30A), one early onset FSHD1 subject (17A), and their unaffected Ctrl family members (15V, 17U, and 30W).
claims.source: For these studies, iMyoblasts were generated by iPSC induction and reserve cell propagation from S3 cultures. iPSCs were reprogrammed from parental CD56+ muscle biopsy cells of six subjects, including two classic FSHD1 subjects (15A and 30A), one early onset FSHD1 subject (17A), and their unaffected Ctrl family members (15V, 17U, and 30W).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the source of cells for scRNA-Seq analysis.

claims.claim: The UMAP plots grouped Ctrl and FSHD1 cells together in each of the five main clusters.
claims.source: The Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots grouped Ctrl and FSHD1 cells together in each of the five main clusters (Figure 2B), as expected as the FSHD1 disease genes are expressed in differentiated myotubes and not in proliferating progenitors.
claims.evidence: UMAP analysis showed clustering of cells by type rather than disease status.

claims.claim: FSHD1 disease genes are expressed in differentiated myotubes and not in proliferating progenitors.
claims.source: The Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots grouped Ctrl and FSHD1 cells together in each of the five main clusters (Figure 2B), as expected as the FSHD1 disease genes are expressed in differentiated myotubes and not in proliferating progenitors.
claims.evidence: The Results section explains why FSHD1 and Ctrl cells cluster together.

claims.claim: UMAP grouped Ctrl and FSHD iMyoblasts into clusters that were distinct from S1, S2, bMyoblast (bMyo), and biopsy mesodermal cell (bMes) clusters.
claims.source: UMAP grouped Ctrl and FSHD iMyoblasts into clusters that were distinct from S1, S2, bMyoblast (bMyo), and biopsy mesodermal cell (bMes) clusters.
claims.evidence: UMAP analysis showed distinct clustering of iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: Each cell type cluster included subsets of cells expressing genes of the different stages of the cell cycle and cells contributed by all six subjects.
claims.source: Each cell type cluster included subsets of cells expressing genes of the different stages of the cell cycle and cells contributed by all six subjects, consistent with a reliable and sensitive UMAP segregation (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: UMAP analysis showed distribution of cell cycle stages and subjects across clusters.

claims.claim: Each of the five clusters had a distinct gene expression signature of myogenic regulatory genes, differentiation genes, and cluster marker genes that further validated their myogenic identities.
claims.source: Each of the five clusters had a distinct gene expression signature of myogenic regulatory genes, differentiation genes, and cluster marker genes that further validated their myogenic identities (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed distinct signatures for each cluster.

claims.claim: The iMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1.
claims.source: The iMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1, the bMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1 as well as PAX7 and MYF5, and the bMes non-myogenic cluster expressed PDGFRA, a mesodermal cell marker (Evseenko et al., 2010; Joe et al., 2010; Uezumi et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed PAX3 and MYOD1 expression in iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: The bMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1 as well as PAX7 and MYF5.
claims.source: The iMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1, the bMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1 as well as PAX7 and MYF5, and the bMes non-myogenic cluster expressed PDGFRA, a mesodermal cell marker (Evseenko et al., 2010; Joe et al., 2010; Uezumi et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed expression of multiple myogenic markers in bMyoblasts.

claims.claim: The bMes non-myogenic cluster expressed PDGFRA, a mesodermal cell marker.
claims.source: The iMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1, the bMyoblast cluster expressed PAX3 and MYOD1 as well as PAX7 and MYF5, and the bMes non-myogenic cluster expressed PDGFRA, a mesodermal cell marker (Evseenko et al., 2010; Joe et al., 2010; Uezumi et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed PDGFRA expression in bMes cells with citations.

claims.claim: bMyo and bMes cells expressed NFIX, a regulator of the switch from embryonic to fetal myogenesis.
claims.source: bMyo and bMes cells expressed NFIX, a regulator of the switch from embryonic to fetal myogenesis (Messina et al., 2010), also expressed by iMyoblasts at lower levels (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed NFIX expression with citation.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts expressed NFIX at lower levels than bMyo and bMes cells.
claims.source: bMyo and bMes cells expressed NFIX, a regulator of the switch from embryonic to fetal myogenesis (Messina et al., 2010), also expressed by iMyoblasts at lower levels (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed lower NFIX expression in iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: Cells in the S1 cluster expressed PAX3 at higher levels than cells in the iMyoblast cluster and expressed LIN28A, which encodes an RNA binding protein controlling self-renewal and differentiation.
claims.source: Cells in the S1 cluster expressed PAX3 at higher levels than cells in the iMyoblast cluster and expressed LIN28A, which encodes an RNA binding protein controlling self-renewal and differentiation (Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013).
claims.evidence: Gene expression analysis showed higher PAX3 and LIN28A expression in S1 cells with citation.

claims.claim: S2 cells had heterogeneous morphology and could be subdivided into a proximal S2A subcluster expressing PAX3 and a more distal S2B subcluster expressing MYOD1, MYOG, and MYH8 muscle differentiation genes, and G1 cell cycle markers.
claims.source: S2 cells had heterogeneous morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and could be subdivided into a proximal S2A subcluster expressing PAX3 and a more distal S2B subcluster expressing MYOD1, MYOG, and MYH8 muscle differentiation genes, and G1 cell cycle markers, consistent with their developmental progression from pre- to post-differentiation stages.
claims.evidence: Gene expression and morphology analysis showed heterogeneity in S2 cells.

claims.claim: These findings establish iMyoblasts as a myogenic cell with a transcriptome distinct from bMyoblasts and S1 and S2 stage myogenic cells.
claims.source: These findings establish iMyoblasts as a myogenic cell with a transcriptome distinct from bMyoblasts and S1 and S2 stage myogenic cells.
claims.evidence: The Results section summarizes the scRNA-Seq findings.

claims.claim: Differences in gene expression between iMyoblasts, bMyoblasts, bMes, S1, S2A, and S2B cell classes were quantitated and subjected to pathway analysis using edgeR.
claims.source: Differences in gene expression between iMyoblasts, bMyoblasts, bMes, S1, S2A, and S2B cell classes were quantitated and subjected to pathway analysis using edgeR (Robinson et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the pathway analysis method with citation.

claims.claim: The 15 pairwise comparisons among the six cell classes each identified at least 4600 differentially expressed coding and non-coding genes at a false discovery rate (FDR)<0.05.
claims.source: The 15 pairwise comparisons among the six cell classes each identified at least 4600 differentially expressed coding and non-coding genes at a false discovery rate (FDR)<0.05 (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: Differential expression analysis identified thousands of differentially expressed genes.

claims.claim: The top-ranked categories for the iMyoblast versus bMyoblast comparison included categories of known myogenic genes, including ECM, focal adhesion, and migration/chemotaxis.
claims.source: The top-ranked categories for the iMyoblast versus bMyoblast comparison included categories of known myogenic genes, including ECM, focal adhesion, and migration/chemotaxis (Gillies and Lieber, 2011; Csapo et al., 2020; Thorsteinsdóttir et al., 2011; Rayagiri et al., 2018), signaling (Chal and Pourquié, 2017), and transcription (Berkes and Tapscott, 2005; Buckingham and Relaix, 2015).
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis identified enriched categories with citations.

claims.claim: Both the upregulated and downregulated genes were significantly enriched for ECM genes, including distinct collagen gene isoforms.
claims.source: Both the upregulated and downregulated genes were significantly enriched for ECM genes, including distinct collagen gene isoforms, with COL4A1, COL4A2, COL4A5, COL4A6, COL8A1, COL11A1, and COL13A1 UP in iMyoblasts compared to bMyoblasts, and COL6A1, COL6A2, COL6A3, COL1A2, COL5A2, COL7A1, COL8A2, and COL22A1 UP in bMyoblasts compared to iMyoblasts.
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis showed enrichment of ECM genes with specific collagen isoforms.

claims.claim: iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts differentially expressed members of matrix processing enzyme gene families, including MMP, ADAMTS, and ADAM, and members of matrix regulatory protein gene families ITG, KRT, CDH, SEMA, and LAM.
claims.source: iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts also differentially expressed members of matrix processing enzyme gene families, including MMP, ADAMTS, and ADAM, and members of matrix regulatory protein gene families ITG, KRT, CDH, SEMA, and LAM, all of which have established regulatory functions during embryonic and adult myogenesis.
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis showed differential expression of matrix-related genes.

claims.claim: Signaling was among the top-ranked GO and KEGG categories and included receptor regulatory activity, receptor ligand activity, and signaling receptor activator activity (enriched among genes UP in bMyoblasts compared to iMyoblasts), and PI3K-Akt, MAPK, Rap1, and Ras pathways (enriched among genes UP in iMyoblasts vs. bMyoblasts).
claims.source: Signaling was among the top-ranked GO and KEGG categories and included receptor regulatory activity, receptor ligand activity, and signaling receptor activator activity (enriched among genes UP in bMyoblasts compared to iMyoblasts), and PI3K-Akt, MAPK, Rap1, and Ras pathways (enriched among genes UP in iMyoblasts vs. bMyoblasts).
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis identified enriched signaling categories.

claims.claim: These pathways include differentially expressed FGF, WNT, and FZD gene family members.
claims.source: These pathways include differentially expressed FGF, WNT, and FZD gene family members.
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis identified specific gene families in signaling pathways.

claims.claim: TGFB, PDGFA, EPHA2 and EPHB2, NOG, IGF2BP1 and IGF2BP3, and HMGA2 were UP in iMyoblasts.
claims.source: Additionally, TGFB, PDGFA, EPHA2 and EPHB2, NOG, IGF2BP1 and IGF2BP3, and HMGA2 were UP in iMyoblasts, while GDNF, VEGFA, BMP4, BMP7, WISP1, SULF1, and GREM2 were UP in bMyoblasts.
claims.evidence: Differential expression analysis identified specific genes upregulated in iMyoblasts.

claims.claim: GDNF, VEGFA, BMP4, BMP7, WISP1, SULF1, and GREM2 were UP in bMyoblasts.
claims.source: Additionally, TGFB, PDGFA, EPHA2 and EPHB2, NOG, IGF2BP1 and IGF2BP3, and HMGA2 were UP in iMyoblasts, while GDNF, VEGFA, BMP4, BMP7, WISP1, SULF1, and GREM2 were UP in bMyoblasts.
claims.evidence: Differential expression analysis identified specific genes upregulated in bMyoblasts.

claims.claim: Transcription categories included DNA-binding transcription activators, for which specific genes UP in bMyoblasts included KLF4, SOX8, SIX2, PITX3, SCX, SNAI1, SNAI2, and SMAD1, and genes UP in iMyoblasts included GATA3, GATA6, HAND2, MEIS2, GLI2, NOTCH1, ETS1, and ETS2.
claims.source: Transcription categories included DNA-binding transcription activators, for which specific genes UP in bMyoblasts included KLF4, SOX8, SIX2, PITX3, SCX, SNAI1, SNAI2, and SMAD1, and genes UP in iMyoblasts included GATA3, GATA6, HAND2, MEIS2, GLI2, NOTCH1, ETS1, and ETS2.
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis identified differentially expressed transcription factors.

claims.claim: The top-ranked KEGG categories for genes UP in bMyoblasts compared to iMyoblasts included mineral absorption, complement and coagulation cascades, arachidonic acid metabolism, and retinoic acid metabolism.
claims.source: The top-ranked KEGG categories for genes UP in bMyoblasts compared to iMyoblasts included mineral absorption, complement and coagulation cascades, arachidonic acid metabolism, and retinoic acid metabolism, whose functions in adult myogenesis are currently unknown.
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis identified enriched KEGG categories.

claims.claim: In all four pairwise comparisons between earlier stages (S1 or S2A) and committed iMyoblasts or bMyoblasts stages, genes UP in the committed myogenic stages are enriched for positive regulation of cell migration and TGFβ signaling.
claims.source: In all four pairwise comparisons between earlier stages (S1 or S2A) and committed iMyoblasts or bMyoblasts stages, genes UP in the committed myogenic stages are enriched for positive regulation of cell migration and TGFβ signaling, while genes UP in the earlier stage are enriched in steroid and cholesterol biosynthesis categories, likely to inhibit replicative stress and replication check point activation leading to cell cycle arrest (Replogle et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis comparing developmental stages identified enriched categories with citation.

claims.claim: Genes UP in the earlier stage are enriched in steroid and cholesterol biosynthesis categories, likely to inhibit replicative stress and replication check point activation leading to cell cycle arrest.
claims.source: In all four pairwise comparisons between earlier stages (S1 or S2A) and committed iMyoblasts or bMyoblasts stages, genes UP in the committed myogenic stages are enriched for positive regulation of cell migration and TGFβ signaling, while genes UP in the earlier stage are enriched in steroid and cholesterol biosynthesis categories, likely to inhibit replicative stress and replication check point activation leading to cell cycle arrest (Replogle et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Pathway analysis identified enriched categories in earlier stages with citation and inference about function.

claims.claim: These findings validate the identity of iMyoblasts as a bona fide PAX3/MYOD1 myogenic cell, distinct both from S1 and S2 cells at early developmental stages of iPSC induction and from adult PAX7/PAX3/MYF5/MYOD1 bMyoblasts.
claims.source: These findings validate the identity of iMyoblasts as a bona fide PAX3/MYOD1 myogenic cell, distinct both from S1 and S2 cells at early developmental stages of iPSC induction and from adult PAX7/PAX3/MYF5/MYOD1 bMyoblasts.
claims.evidence: The Results section summarizes the pathway analysis findings.

claims.claim: The differentiation of Ctrl, FSHD1, and LGMDR7 iMyoblasts was compared in cultures using growth factor-free N2 medium to induce myotube differentiation.
claims.source: The differentiation of Ctrl, FSHD1, and LGMDR7 iMyoblasts was compared in cultures using growth factor-free N2 medium to induce myotube differentiation.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the differentiation assay method.

claims.claim: iMyotube cultures from these iMyoblasts upregulated CKM and MYH8 muscle genes with similar kinetics, as determined by qPCR assays.
claims.source: iMyotube cultures from these iMyoblasts upregulated CKM and MYH8 muscle genes with similar kinetics, as determined by qPCR assays (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed upregulation of muscle genes during differentiation.

claims.claim: iMyotubes expressed low levels of adult MYH1 compared to bMyotubes, consistent with their identity as a fetal/embryonic lineage.
claims.source: iMyotubes expressed low levels of adult MYH1 compared to bMyotubes (Figure 4A), consistent with their identity as a fetal/embryonic lineage.
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed lower MYH1 expression in iMyotubes compared to bMyotubes.

claims.claim: Ctrl and FSHD1 iMyotubes similarly upregulated the expression of muscle genes in both N2 and Opti-MEM growth factor-free media.
claims.source: Ctrl and FSHD1 iMyotubes similarly upregulated the expression of muscle genes in both N2 and Opti-MEM growth factor-free media (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed similar upregulation in different media.

claims.claim: Expression levels of myogenic regulators PAX3, MYOD1, and MYOG and CKM and MYH8 differentiation genes varied by cell line but were not specifically impacted by whether iMyoblasts were derived from iPSCs reprogrammed from fibroblasts or bMyoblast parental cells.
claims.source: Expression levels of myogenic regulators PAX3, MYOD1, and MYOG and CKM and MYH8 differentiation genes varied by cell line but were not specifically impacted by whether iMyoblasts were derived from iPSCs reprogrammed from fibroblasts or bMyoblast parental cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: qPCR data showed variation by cell line but not by parental cell type.

claims.claim: All three supplemented N2 media significantly increased expression of MYH7, MYH8, and CKM in Ctrl and FSHD1 iMyotubes, but not adult MYH1.
claims.source: All three supplemented N2 media significantly increased expression of MYH7, MYH8, and CKM in Ctrl and FSHD1 iMyotubes, but not adult MYH1, which as previously shown was expressed at high levels by bMyotubes except in N2+ SB + De + Da + F medium, which inhibited bMyoblast fusion and differentiation markers, but not MYOD1 and PAX3 expression (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: NanoString data showed increased expression of specific muscle genes in supplemented media.

claims.claim: N2+ SB + De + Da + F medium inhibited bMyoblast fusion and differentiation markers, but not MYOD1 and PAX3 expression.
claims.source: All three supplemented N2 media significantly increased expression of MYH7, MYH8, and CKM in Ctrl and FSHD1 iMyotubes, but not adult MYH1, which as previously shown was expressed at high levels by bMyotubes except in N2+ SB + De + Da + F medium, which inhibited bMyoblast fusion and differentiation markers, but not MYOD1 and PAX3 expression (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: NanoString data and images showed inhibition of differentiation but not myogenic markers in specific medium.

claims.claim: Increased muscle RNA expression in iMyotubes was correlated with increased networks of multinucleated myotubes, most prevalent in N2 + SB + P + C medium.
claims.source: Increased muscle RNA expression in iMyotubes was correlated with increased networks of multinucleated myotubes, most prevalent in N2 + SB + P + C medium (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: NanoString data and images showed correlation between RNA expression and myotube formation.

claims.claim: The expression of myogenic regulators MYOD1 and PAX3 was variable, but their expression was not differentially affected by these media, showing that their effects are on differentiation and not myogenic commitment.
claims.source: The expression of myogenic regulators MYOD1 and PAX3 was variable, but their expression was not differentially affected by these media, showing that their effects are on differentiation and not myogenic commitment.
claims.evidence: NanoString data showed variable but not differentially affected expression of myogenic regulators.

claims.claim: bMyoblast expression of muscle RNAs was increased in response to N2+ SB medium, particularly for FSHD1 bMyoblasts, likely by reducing DUX4-mediated toxicity.
claims.source: By contrast, bMyoblast expression of muscle RNAs was increased in response to N2+ SB medium, particularly for FSHD1 bMyoblasts, likely by reducing DUX4-mediated toxicity.
claims.evidence: NanoString data showed increased muscle RNA expression in bMyoblasts in N2+SB medium with inference about mechanism.

claims.claim: N2 + SB + P + C medium showed lower-level muscle RNA expression and N2 + SB + De + Da + F medium completely blocked muscle RNA expression and bMyoblast fusion.
claims.source: However, N2 + SB + P + C medium showed lower-level muscle RNA expression and N2 + SB + De + Da + F medium completely blocked muscle RNA expression and bMyoblast fusion (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: NanoString data and images showed reduced or blocked muscle RNA expression and fusion in specific media.

claims.claim: These findings reveal that iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts, and FSHD and Ctrl cells, respond differently to specialized differentiation media, reflecting their underlying differences in operative signaling mechanisms and toxicity responses.
claims.source: These findings reveal that iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts, and FSHD and Ctrl cells, respond differently to specialized differentiation media, reflecting their underlying differences in operative signaling mechanisms and toxicity responses.
claims.evidence: The Results section summarizes the differentiation findings.

claims.claim: DUX4 is a primate-specific member of the double homeobox (DUX) family of transcription factor genes of eutherian mammals, located in the D4Z4 retrotransposon repeat array near the telomere of chromosome 4.
claims.source: DUX4 is a primate-specific member of the double homeobox (DUX) family of transcription factor genes of eutherian mammals, located in the D4Z4 retrotransposon repeat array near the telomere of chromosome 4 (Gabriëls et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes DUX4 with citation.

claims.claim: DUX4 developmentally functions to coordinate zygotic genome activation and male germline differentiation.
claims.source: DUX4 developmentally functions to coordinate zygotic genome activation and male germline differentiation (DeSimone et al., 2017).

results.result: A transgene-free protocol was developed to generate iMyoblasts from iPSCs through a three-stage myogenic induction process that sequentially upregulates PAX3, MYOD1, and MYH8 expression, achieving ~1000-fold upregulation of these markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C18-C22 describe the protocol development and validation. The sequential upregulation of myogenic markers (PAX3, MYOD1, MYH8) is demonstrated by qPCR data (C21-C22) and immunofluorescence (C23-C24), with consistent results across multiple iPSC and ESC lines from control and disease subjects. The protocol is well-characterized with appropriate molecular validation.

results.result: The three-stage induction protocol produces cultures with 90% MYOD1+ cells at S2 stage and 80% MF20+ mononucleated iMyocytes at S3 stage, with PAX7 expression 100-fold lower than PAX3.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data showing high percentages of marker-positive cells. The low PAX7 expression is consistent with cited literature on transgene-free protocols (C27). The comparison to embryonic myogenic cells (C25) is appropriately cited and represents a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: iMyoblasts express PAX3 and MYOD1 (but not PAX7), proliferate with 12-hour doubling times, can be expanded for >12 passages (>30 population doublings) while maintaining myogenic markers and differentiation capacity, and fuse to form multinucleated myotubes.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by qPCR data (C28-C29), proliferation assays (C30), passage experiments with marker expression and differentiation assays (C31), and immunofluorescence showing myotube formation (C32). The data demonstrate stable maintenance of myogenic identity over extended culture, which is a key characteristic for utility in research applications.

results.result: iMyoblasts express fetal and adult myogenic cell surface markers (CD82, CD56, CD318, ERBB3, NGFR), and both CD82+/CD56+ and CD82+/CD56− populations can differentiate into myotubes. iMyoblasts retain dual commitment to differentiation and reserve cell regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by flow cytometry data (C33), FAC-sorting experiments with differentiation assays (C34), and reserve cell selection experiments (C35). The demonstration that sorted populations retain differentiation capacity validates the myogenic commitment of CD82+ cells. The dual commitment to differentiation and reserve cell generation is a key stem cell characteristic.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of iMyoblasts, bMyoblasts, S1, S2, and biopsy cells from six subjects (3 FSHD1, 3 control) identified distinct transcriptional clusters. iMyoblasts express PAX3 and MYOD1 (but not PAX7 or MYF5), while bMyoblasts express PAX3, MYOD1, PAX7, and MYF5. S2 cells subdivide into PAX3+ (S2A) and MYOD1+/MYOG+/MYH8+ (S2B) subclusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C50 describe comprehensive scRNA-seq analysis with appropriate UMAP clustering, cell cycle analysis, and gene expression profiling. The clustering of FSHD1 and control cells together (C38) is appropriately explained by the fact that disease genes are expressed in differentiated cells, not progenitors (C39). The distinct gene expression signatures for each cluster (C42-C49) establish iMyoblasts as a unique myogenic cell type. The analysis includes cells from all six subjects across cell cycle stages, supporting robust clustering.

results.result: Pathway analysis using edgeR identified >4600 differentially expressed genes (FDR<0.05) in pairwise comparisons between cell types. iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts differentially express genes in ECM, focal adhesion, migration, signaling (PI3K-Akt, MAPK, Rap1, Ras), and transcription categories. Committed myogenic stages (iMyoblasts, bMyoblasts) show enrichment for cell migration and TGFβ signaling compared to earlier stages (S1, S2A).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C64 describe comprehensive pathway analysis with appropriate statistical methods (edgeR) and multiple testing correction (FDR<0.05). The identification of thousands of differentially expressed genes with enrichment in biologically relevant pathways (ECM, signaling, transcription) is well-supported. The analysis includes specific gene examples (C54, C58-C60) and appropriate citations for pathway functions. The comparison between developmental stages (C62-C63) provides biological context. However, the authors appropriately note potential batch effects and biases in the methods section.

results.result: Control, FSHD1, and LGMDR7 iMyoblasts differentiate with similar kinetics in N2 medium, upregulating CKM and MYH8. iMyotubes express low levels of adult MYH1 compared to bMyotubes, consistent with a fetal/embryonic lineage. Expression levels vary by cell line but not by parental cell type (fibroblast vs. bMyoblast origin).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by qPCR data comparing differentiation across multiple cell lines and conditions. The low MYH1 expression in iMyotubes compared to bMyotubes (C67) supports the fetal-like identity. The finding that parental cell type does not impact differentiation (C69) is important for protocol generalizability. The similar differentiation kinetics across disease and control lines validates the protocol's consistency.

results.result: Supplemented N2 media (N2+SB+P+C, N2+SB+De+Da+F) increase expression of MYH7, MYH8, and CKM in iMyotubes but not adult MYH1. N2+SB+De+Da+F inhibits bMyoblast fusion and differentiation markers but not MYOD1/PAX3. iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts respond differently to specialized differentiation media.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 are supported by NanoString data and microscopy images showing differential responses to media supplements. The uncoupling of myogenic commitment (MYOD1/PAX3) from differentiation markers in specific media (C71, C73) is an important mechanistic finding. The differential responses between iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts (C76) reflect underlying biological differences. However, the mechanistic explanations (e.g., C74 about DUX4-mediated toxicity) are inferences rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: DUX4 is a primate-specific transcription factor located in the D4Z4 repeat array on chromosome 4 that functions in zygotic genome activation and is normally repressed in non-germline tissues. FSHD is caused by DUX4 misexpression due to D4Z4 contraction (FSHD1) or chromatin-modifying gene mutations (FSHD2), leading to muscle toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C84 provide background on DUX4 and FSHD with appropriate citations to established literature. These are knowledge claims that set context for the experimental findings. The claims accurately represent the current understanding of FSHD pathogenesis as supported by the cited references.

results.result: FSHD1 iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts upregulate DUX4 target genes >1000-fold during differentiation, with bMyoblasts showing 24-hour delayed upregulation compared to iMyoblasts. DUX4-GFP reporter shows expression in 4/100 FSHD1 iMyotube nuclei, with 10× higher frequency in iMyoblasts than bMyoblasts, suggesting more stringent DUX4 repression in bMyoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C91 are supported by qPCR data showing robust upregulation of DUX4 target genes and DUX4-GFP reporter assays quantifying nuclear expression frequency. The delayed upregulation in bMyoblasts (C86) with similar differentiation kinetics (C87) supports the inference of more stringent repression in bMyoblasts. The 10× higher frequency in iMyoblasts (C91) is a quantitative observation, though the inference about repression mechanisms requires additional validation. The parental cell type independence (C88) is important for protocol generalizability.

results.result: Media supplements differentially affect DUX4 target gene expression: N2 medium shows highest expression in iMyotubes, while N2+SB+P+C and N2+SB+De+Da+F dramatically reduce DUX4 target genes (likely via corticosteroids), uncoupling DUX4 expression from muscle differentiation. Both iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts respond to Losmapimod (p38 inhibitor), indicating shared DUX4 regulatory pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 are supported by NanoString data showing differential effects of media supplements on DUX4 target genes versus muscle genes. The uncoupling of DUX4 from differentiation (C93) is an important finding for understanding FSHD pathogenesis. The mechanistic explanation involving corticosteroids (C96) is appropriately cited. The Losmapimod response (C97) validates the disease model and suggests therapeutic potential. However, the mechanistic inferences about corticosteroid action are not directly tested.

results.result: DUX4 and target genes are not upregulated during S3 differentiation or earlier S1/S2 stages of iPSC/ESC myogenic induction, despite being upregulated >1000-fold in differentiating iMyoblasts/bMyoblasts. DUX4 levels in FSHD1 iPSCs/ESCs are 100-fold lower than in differentiating myoblasts. These findings contradict Caron et al., 2016.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by qPCR and NanoString data showing lack of DUX4 upregulation during early stages despite robust upregulation in iMyoblasts. The explicit contradiction with Caron et al., 2016 (C102) is appropriately noted, and the authors qualify their findings (C103) by not excluding low-level upregulation. The 100-fold difference between iPSCs/ESCs and differentiating myoblasts (C101) is a substantial quantitative finding that supports the conclusion of developmental repression.

results.result: DUX4 4qA alleles remain hypomethylated (~20% CpG methylation) in FSHD1 cells and hypermethylated (~60%) in control cells throughout iPSC reprogramming, myogenic induction (S1-S3), and iMyoblast/iMyotube stages. These findings contradict Dion et al., 2019, which used non-4qA-specific primers that obscure distal 4qA hypomethylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by bisulfite sequencing data using 4qA-specific primers across multiple stages and cell lines. The maintenance of methylation states (C105) is a key finding showing that methylation changes do not account for DUX4 repression. The contradiction with Dion et al., 2019 (C107) is appropriately explained by methodological differences in primer specificity (C108). The use of 4qA-specific primers is a critical technical detail that strengthens the findings.

results.result: The MYOD1 core enhancer becomes hypermethylated during iPSC reprogramming and demethylated during myogenic induction/differentiation, concordant with MYOD1 RNA upregulation. This demonstrates that methylation machinery is operative in iPSCs and induced myogenic cells, but contracted 4qA alleles are refractory to this machinery. Therefore, methylation changes cannot account for DUX4 repression in FSHD1 iPSCs/ESCs/S3 iMyocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing dynamic methylation changes at the MYOD1 locus that correlate with gene expression. This control experiment (C109) demonstrates that the methylation machinery is functional, strengthening the conclusion that 4qA alleles are refractory (C110). The inference that methylation changes cannot account for DUX4 repression (C111) is logical given the maintained hypomethylation of 4qA alleles. This is a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: 5-azacytidine (5-AzaC) treatment increases DUX4 expression in FSHD1 S3 myocyte cultures in a concentration-dependent manner to levels comparable to iMyoblasts/bMyoblasts. This shows DUX4 repression is mediated by 5-AzaC-sensitive DNA methylation of a DUX4 regulatory locus that becomes inoperative in FSHD1 iMyoblasts/bMyoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by qPCR data showing dose-dependent DUX4 upregulation with 5-AzaC treatment. The inference about a 5-AzaC-sensitive regulatory locus (C113) is reasonable given the data, though the specific locus is not identified. This is a novel mechanistic finding revealing a previously unknown epigenetic regulatory mechanism for DUX4 repression during development. However, the identity and location of the regulatory locus require further investigation.

results.result: iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts xenoengraft into irradiated and BaCl2-injured NSG mouse TA muscle, forming humanized ECM domains with human nuclei and muscle fibers. Spectrin β1+ fibers appear within 2 weeks, increase by 4 weeks, and are more numerous in bMyoblast than iMyoblast xenografts. FSHD1 xenografts have fewer fibers than control, likely due to DUX4-mediated toxicity. Xenografts express muscle genes (MYH8, CKM) at comparable levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C123 are supported by immunofluorescence data with human-specific antibodies, qPCR data, and quantification of fiber numbers. The formation of humanized domains (C115-C116) and time-dependent increase in fibers (C118) demonstrate successful engraftment and differentiation. The lower fiber numbers in FSHD1 xenografts (C119) with inference about DUX4 toxicity is reasonable given the known pathology. The validation of irradiation effectiveness (C122) is an important control. The presence of mouse endothelial cells (C123) is expected for vascular reconstruction.

results.result: Xenoengraftment efficiency assessed by human/mouse RNA ratios shows bMyoblast xenografts are 20-60% human (RPL13A) and 40-60% human (MYH2), while iMyoblast xenografts are 5-20% human (RPL13A) and 20-25% human (MYH2). The lower RPL13A percentage likely reflects abundant non-muscle mouse cells. iMyoblasts xenoengraft efficiently for muscle maturation and regeneration studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 are supported by NanoString data quantifying human/mouse RNA ratios. The explanation for lower RPL13A percentages (C126) is a reasonable inference about cell composition. The conclusion about efficient engraftment (C127) is supported by the data, though iMyoblasts show lower efficiency than bMyoblasts. The differential expression of ECM and matrix genes (C128) provides a mechanistic basis for engraftment differences, though this is an inference requiring further validation.

results.result: Ex vivo, iMyotubes and bMyotubes express high MYH3 (embryonic/fetal) and intermediate MYH7/MYH8, with iMyotubes expressing low MYH1/MYH2 compared to bMyotubes. In vivo, 2-4 week iMyoblast xenografts downregulate MYH3/MYH7/MYH8 up to 100-fold and upregulate adult fast MYH1/MYH2 >100-fold, demonstrating fetal-to-adult MYH isoform switching and regulatory plasticity in response to host muscle signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C135 are supported by NanoString data showing dramatic MYH isoform switching in xenografts. The 100-fold changes in expression (C131) are substantial and clearly demonstrate developmental maturation. The similar but lesser switching in bMyoblast xenografts (C133) and unchanged MYH4 (C134) provide important context. The conclusion about regulatory plasticity (C135) is well-supported by the data and appropriately cited. This is a key finding demonstrating that iMyoblasts can respond to adult muscle environmental signals.

results.result: LGMDR7 iMyoblasts (with 8bp TCAP microduplication) undergo muscle differentiation ex vivo and in xenografts. Telethonin expression can be efficiently restored by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated microhomology repair, establishing utility for gene editing therapeutics.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C140 are supported by qPCR data, immunofluorescence, and citation to previous gene editing work (Iyer et al., 2019). The disease background (C136-C137) is appropriately described. The differentiation capacity (C138) validates the disease model. The gene editing result (C139) is cited from previous work, and the inference about therapeutic utility (C140) is reasonable. However, the gene editing data is not shown in this manuscript, relying on citation.

results.result: S1 stage FSHD1 cells engraft poorly and do not differentiate well compared to iMyoblast xenografts, as evidenced by high qPCR Ct values comparable to unengrafted mouse TA. This highlights the efficiency of iMyoblast engraftment for in vivo studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142 are supported by qPCR data showing poor engraftment of S1 cells. This negative control (C141) strengthens the conclusion about iMyoblast engraftment efficiency (C142). The comparison to unengrafted muscle provides appropriate context for interpreting the Ct values.

results.result: WWS and LGMDR9 iMyoblasts (with FKRP mutations causing α-dystroglycan glycosylation defects) xenoengraft efficiently and express muscle RNAs. WWS iMyotubes show almost complete absence of laminin binding and IIH6 reactivity with unglycosylated α-DG (75 kDa), while LGMDR9 shows intermediate binding/glycosylation, modeling the functional and clinical severity of FKRP mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C150 are supported by immunofluorescence, qPCR, laminin binding assays, and Western blots. The disease background (C143-C145) is appropriately described. The efficient xenoengraftment (C146) validates the model. The laminin binding assays (C147) and Western blot data (C148) demonstrate dose-dependent loss of function correlating with disease severity. The conclusion that glycosylation differences model disease severity (C149) is well-supported. This provides a well-characterized disease model for therapeutic development (C150).

results.result: Primary xenografts of control and WWS iMyoblasts contain PAX3+/lamin A/C+ nuclei associated with human muscle fibers. After secondary BaCl2 injury, PAX3+ nuclei and differentiated human muscle fibers (neonatal MHC+, collagen VI+, laminin β1+) are observed in humanized areas, demonstrating that iMyoblast xenografts maintain PAX3+ myogenic cells that regenerate human muscle in response to injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C156 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing PAX3+ nuclei in primary xenografts and after secondary injury, along with markers of differentiated muscle. The co-localization with human-specific markers (C152) confirms the human origin of PAX3+ cells. The presence of differentiated muscle after secondary injury (C155) demonstrates regenerative capacity. The conclusion about maintained PAX3+ progenitors with regenerative function (C156) is well-supported by the data. This is a key finding for stem cell therapeutic potential.

results.result: The iMyoblast protocol has been successfully applied to control and disease (FSHD1, WWS, LGMDR7, LGMDR9) iPSCs. The protocol differs from others by using efficient reserve cell selection without FAC sorting. iMyoblasts can be expanded for ≥30 population doublings while retaining differentiation capacity, enabling statistically powered studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C160 summarize the protocol's broad applicability and advantages. The successful application to multiple disease lines (C157) is demonstrated throughout the manuscript. The unique feature of reserve cell selection without FAC sorting (C158) is a methodological advantage. The expansion capacity (C159) is supported by data in C31. The inference about enabling powered studies (C160) is reasonable given the expansion capacity, though specific power calculations are not provided.

results.result: Adult bMyoblasts often cannot be propagated from dystrophy patients with advanced pathology due to senescence. iPSC-derived iMyoblasts enable mechanistic studies of epigenetic disease mechanisms, as demonstrated by discovery of developmental DUX4 repression. iMyoblasts undergo enhanced differentiation in specialized media, enabling 3D modeling of muscle maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 are discussion points summarizing advantages of iMyoblasts. The limitation of adult bMyoblasts (C161) is appropriately cited. The advantage for epigenetic studies (C162) is demonstrated by the DUX4 findings. The potential for 3D modeling (C163) is speculative about future applications based on the enhanced differentiation data, which is reasonable but not directly demonstrated in this study.

results.result: iMyoblasts express fetal myoblast markers (PAX3, CD82, NFIX) and have a transcriptome distinct from S1/S2 progenitors (which lack NFIX and differentiate as mononucleated myocytes) and from adult bMyoblasts (which express PAX7, MYF5, MRF4, and higher NFIX). The iMyoblast transcriptome shares fetal-like gene expression profiles with limb myogenic developmental trajectories.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C167 synthesize the characterization data to define iMyoblast identity. The expression of fetal markers (C164) is supported by flow cytometry and scRNA-seq data. The distinctions from S1/S2 cells (C165) and bMyoblasts (C166) are supported by the transcriptome analysis. The comparison to developmental trajectories (C167) is appropriately cited (Xi et al., 2020). This provides a clear developmental context for iMyoblast identity.

results.result: iMyoblasts may be related to adult PAX3+ myogenic cells in diaphragm or stress-resistant PAX3+ cells. In humans, PAX3 and PAX7 may be functionally redundant, as PAX7 is not essential for satellite cell production and regeneration. iMyoblasts express transcription factors (GATA3, GATA6, HAND2, MEIS2, GLI2, NOTCH1, ETS1, ETS2) that likely regulate ECM, focal adhesion, migration, and signaling genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C170 are speculative discussion points. The relationship to adult PAX3+ cells (C168) is appropriately cited but not directly tested. The PAX3/PAX7 redundancy (C169) is cited from other work. The regulatory role of transcription factors (C170) is an inference from expression data without functional validation. These are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but lack direct experimental support in this study.

results.result: iMyoblasts express embryonic/fetal MYH8 ex vivo but undergo MYH isoform switching to adult fast MYH1 in xenografts, demonstrating transcriptional plasticity to respond to in vivo signals. The signals initiating adult switching may be controlled by innervation or conversion to adult-like progenitor phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C172 are supported by the MYH isoform switching data (C129-C135). The demonstration of plasticity (C172) is a key finding. The speculation about mechanisms (C173) is appropriately qualified as uncertain and cites relevant literature (Xi et al., 2020). The mechanistic hypotheses are reasonable but require further investigation.

results.result: iMyoblasts have stem cell characteristics (dual commitment to differentiation and reserve cell renewal ex vivo, regeneration capacity in vivo) that likely reflect their isolation by reserve cell selection from S3 cultures. The mechanisms controlling reserve cell generation are not understood but likely involve MYOD1 autoregulation during S1/S2 induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C178 synthesize the stem cell characteristics demonstrated throughout the manuscript. The dual commitment (C175) is supported by reserve cell selection experiments (C35) and regeneration data (C151-C156). The inference about isolation method (C176) is reasonable and appropriately cited. The speculation about MYOD1 autoregulation (C178) is appropriately qualified as uncertain and cited. The acknowledgment that mechanisms are not understood (C178) is appropriate.

results.result: iMyoblasts maintain low-level MYOD1 and PAX3 expression cell-autonomously, enabling myogenic potential over 30 population doublings and dual commitment to differentiation and reserve cell renewal. The regulatory mechanisms are not understood, but iMyoblasts express genes known to regulate MYOD1 function, differentiation, and self-renewal (ID genes, DKK1, GREM1, RGS4, TXNRD1, UCHL1, NR2F2, FOXC2, HMGA2, IGF2BP).
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C183 synthesize the expansion and maintenance data. The cell-autonomous maintenance of markers (C179) is supported by passage experiments (C31). The in vivo behavior (C180) is supported by xenograft data. The acknowledgment that mechanisms are not understood (C181) is appropriate. The expression of regulatory genes (C182) is supported by scRNA-seq data with appropriate citations. The suggestion of CRISPR studies (C183) is a reasonable future direction.

results.result: The findings establish a protocol for iMyoblast isolation suitable for ex vivo and in vivo investigations of human myogenesis and disease pathogenesis. iMyoblasts are expected to enable development of gene editing and stem cell therapeutics for muscular dystrophies.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C185 are summary statements. The establishment of the protocol (C184) is well-supported by the comprehensive characterization throughout the manuscript. The expectation about therapeutic applications (C185) is appropriately qualified as speculative but is reasonable given the demonstrated characteristics (expansion capacity, gene editing responsiveness, engraftment, regeneration). This represents a logical conclusion from the presented data.

results.result: The authors developed a two-step transgene-free protocol to generate iMyoblasts from iPSCs using commercially available reagents. The protocol involves sequential upregulation of PAX3, MYOD1, and MYH8 through three stages (S1, S2, S3), with robust 1000-fold upregulation of these markers validated across multiple control and disease iPSC/ESC lines.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges 'a capacity for the iPSC Myoblasts to be generated and their commitment to form viable primary lines' and notes the study demonstrates successful generation using the protocol. Reviewer 2 does not challenge the protocol itself but requests validation with the newer Myocea kit, indicating acceptance of the methodology while seeking broader validation.

results.result: iMyoblasts are characterized as a PAX3+/MYOD1+ skeletal myogenic lineage distinct from adult bMyoblasts (which express PAX7, MYF5 in addition to PAX3/MYOD1) and from S1/S2 stage progenitors. Immunofluorescence showed 90% MYOD1+ cells in S2 and 80% MF20+ cells in S3 cultures. Flow cytometry demonstrated expression of fetal/adult myogenic surface markers (CD82, CD56, CD318, ERBB3, NGFR).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 accepts that 'iPSC myoblasts constituting a specific lineage, reflected in their transcriptosomes.' However, Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns: 'Pax 3 and MyoD not quantified at the protein level' and notes 'Figure 2: lack of IF quantifications (MyoD, pax3, pax7, fusion index…).' The reviewers request protein-level quantification rather than accepting RNA-level data alone.

results.result: iMyoblasts can be stably propagated for >12 passages or 30 population doublings with 12-hour doubling times while maintaining expression of PAX3 and MYOD1 and commitment to differentiate.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes the study demonstrates 'a capacity for the iPSC Myoblasts to be generated and their commitment to form viable primary lines committed to differentiate in Opti–MEM serum free medium.' Reviewer 2 does not challenge the expansion capacity claims.

results.result: iMyoblasts fuse to form multinucleated iMyotubes during differentiation and retain dual commitment to both differentiate and generate reserve cells that can be recovered as MYOD1+ iMyoblasts (tMyoblasts).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically critiques: 'Fusion stated to be a key difference between iMyoblasts and S3 cells, but not quantified' and 'Tertiary reserve population experiment not quantified.' The reviewers accept the observation but require quantification to fully support the claims.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing defined the iMyoblast transcriptome as distinct from bMyoblasts, S1, S2, and biopsy mesodermal cells. UMAP analysis grouped cells into five main clusters with distinct gene expression signatures. Pathway analysis identified at least 4600 differentially expressed genes between cell classes, with enrichment in ECM, focal adhesion, migration/chemotaxis, signaling, and transcription categories.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 accepts that 'iPSC myoblasts constituting a specific lineage, reflected in their transcriptosomes.' However, Reviewer 2 states 'Figure 3: conclusion/take home message unclear,' indicating the reviewers found the transcriptome analysis difficult to interpret despite not directly challenging the data quality.

results.result: iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts differentiate with similar kinetics of muscle gene upregulation (CKM, MYH8) but iMyotubes express low levels of adult MYH1 compared to bMyotubes. Specialized differentiation media (N2+SB+P+C, N2+SB+De+Da+F) differentially affect iMyoblasts versus bMyoblasts, with enhanced muscle gene expression in iMyotubes but variable effects on bMyotubes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'In Material and Methods it is said that a differentiation of 2 to 7 days was performed. This sounds like a rather wide spectrum. Cells differentiated for 3 days could show a profile quite different from cells that have been kept in differentiation for 7 days.' This raises concerns about the consistency and interpretation of differentiation timing, though the data itself is not directly challenged.

results.result: FSHD1 iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts both upregulated DUX4 target genes >1000-fold during differentiation, with iMyoblasts showing earlier upregulation (24hr earlier) than bMyoblasts. DUX4-GFP reporter showed 4/100 nuclei expressing DUX4 in FSHD1 iMyotubes, 10× higher frequency than bMyoblasts. Media supplements differentially affected DUX4 expression, and both cell types responded to Losmapimod (p38 inhibitor).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The section on FSHD is perhaps overly technical and difficult to digest for non specialists. It was complicated to grasp what the actual advance is in terms of in vitro FSHD modelling' and requests 'FSHD– please clarify take home message and quantify Dux4 from reporter cell line.' The reviewers accept the data but find the significance and novelty unclear.

results.result: DUX4 and target genes were not upregulated during S1, S2, or S3 stages of myogenic induction, contradicting Caron et al. 2016. DUX4 4qA alleles remained hypomethylated in FSHD1 iPSCs/ESCs and throughout differentiation stages, contradicting Dion et al. 2019. MYOD1 core enhancer underwent methylation changes during reprogramming and differentiation. 5-azacytidine treatment increased DUX4 expression in S3 myocytes, indicating methylation-mediated repression at a regulatory locus distinct from the 4qA DUX4 locus.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the FSHD section is 'overly technical and difficult to digest' and requests clarification of the 'actual advance in terms of in vitro FSHD modelling.' While the reviewers do not directly challenge the methylation data or the contradiction with previous studies, they express difficulty understanding the significance and request clearer presentation of the take-home message.

results.result: iMyoblasts and bMyoblasts efficiently xenoengrafted into irradiated and injured mouse TA muscle, forming humanized ECM domains with human nuclei and muscle fibers. Spectrin β1+ fibers were detectable within 2 weeks and increased by 4 weeks. FSHD1 xenografts had fewer fibers than controls. Engraftment efficiency was 5-20% human (iMyoblasts) and 20-60% human (bMyoblasts) by RPL13A assays, and 20-25% (iMyoblasts) and 40-60% (bMyoblasts) by MYH2 assays.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 accepts that 'iPSC myoblasts constituting a specific lineage, reflected in their...xenograft properties.' However, Reviewer 2 requests 'No quantification of LAMIN A/C & SPECTRIN double positive donor derived fibers provided. – please quantify.' The reviewers accept the xenograft data but require more rigorous quantification.

results.result: iMyoblast xenografts underwent fetal-to-adult MYH isoform switching, downregulating embryonic/fetal MYH3, MYH7, MYH8 by up to 100-fold and upregulating adult fast MYH1 and MYH2 by >100-fold at 2-4 weeks post-engraftment. This demonstrates regulatory plasticity to respond to signals in the adult host muscle.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes the study demonstrates 'iPSC myoblasts constituting a specific lineage, reflected in their...xenograft properties.' Reviewer 2 does not challenge the MYH isoform switching data, and the quantitative nature of the findings (100-fold changes) addresses potential concerns about rigor.

results.result: Primary xenografts maintained PAX3+ nuclei in humanized regions, and secondary injury induced regeneration with PAX3+/lamin A/C+ nuclei and differentiated muscle fibers (neonatal MHC+, collagen VI+, laminin β1+), demonstrating that xenografts maintain a progenitor population capable of regenerating human muscle.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests 'Given the capacity of forming reserve cells, the expectation in this study was to see this finding validated also in vivo with serial injuries or transplantation, as well as quantification of contribution to satellite cell pool – please quantify donor derived Pax7+ cells in vivo and perform serial injury or transplantation study and quantification.' The reviewers accept the observation but require more extensive validation and quantification, particularly for PAX7+ cells.

results.result: LGMDR7 iMyoblasts (with TCAP 8bp microduplication) undergo muscle differentiation ex vivo and in xenografts. Previous work showed Telethonin expression could be restored by CRISPR gene editing, establishing utility for therapeutic development.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'LGMDR7: this section appears out of context and brief.' The reviewers do not challenge the data but find the presentation insufficient and the connection to the overall narrative unclear.

results.result: WWS and LGMDR9 iMyoblasts (FKRP dystroglycanopathies) xenoengraft efficiently and express muscle genes. Ex vivo assays showed WWS iMyotubes had almost complete absence of laminin binding and were deficient in IIH6 reactivity with smaller unglycosylated α-DG (75 kDa) compared to glycosylated control (100 kDa), while LGMDR9 showed intermediate phenotypes, modeling the functional and clinical severity of FKRP mutations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'FKRP: in this case the novelty is limited (e.g. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31566294/) and the reported findings are very limited in terms of disease modelling.' The reviewers accept the data but question the novelty and significance of the disease modeling, citing prior work.

results.result: S1 stage cells engrafted poorly compared to iMyoblasts, with high raw Ct values comparable to unengrafted mouse TA samples, highlighting the efficiency and utility of iMyoblasts for in vivo studies.
results.evaluation: Neither reviewer challenges this comparative finding. The data serves to validate the superiority of the iMyoblast protocol over earlier stage cells for xenograft studies.

results.result: The iMyoblast protocol has been successfully applied to multiple disease iPSC lines (FSHD1, WWS, LGMDR7, LGMDR9) and differs from other protocols by efficient reserve cell selection without FAC sorting. The expandable nature enables statistically powered studies, and advantages include discovery of novel epigenetic mechanisms (DUX4 repression) and potential for therapeutic development including gene editing and stem cell therapies.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 concludes 'The authors thus have developed a successful and efficient and reliable method to isolate iPSC myoblasts. This is an attractive and thorough study.' However, Reviewer 2 questions 'it is unclear what the key advantage over other methods and over the commercial kit is' and notes 'The expectation from such a method would have been to have more mature, adult–like myogenic progenitors...However, this appears not to be the case, as Pax7 remains low.' The reviewers are divided on whether the advantages are sufficiently demonstrated.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the protocol development and validation (C1, C18, C20-C22). Peer reviewers also accept the protocol's success, with Reviewer 1 acknowledging 'capacity for iPSC Myoblasts to be generated' and Reviewer 2 requesting validation with newer kits but not challenging the methodology itself. Both SUPPORTED.

Disagreement on sufficiency of evidence.

Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 noting 'viable primary lines committed to differentiate' and neither reviewer challenging expansion claims. Agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 specifically requesting: 'Fusion stated to be a key difference...but not quantified' and 'Tertiary reserve population experiment not quantified.' Disagreement on whether quantification is sufficient.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'differentiation of 2 to 7 days...sounds like a rather wide spectrum' and expressing concern about consistency of differentiation timing. Disagreement on whether timing variability affects interpretation.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to concerns about differentiation timing variability (2-7 days), which could affect interpretation of media supplement effects.

Both evaluate DUX4 upregulation in FSHD models (C85-C91 in OpenEval; C85-C99 in peer review). OpenEval finds qPCR and reporter assay data SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating the FSHD section is 'overly technical and difficult to digest for non specialists' and requesting clarification of 'actual advance in terms of in vitro FSHD modelling.' Disagreement on clarity and significance rather than data quality.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, finding the FSHD section difficult to interpret and requesting quantification of Dux4 from reporter cell line. Disagreement on sufficiency of presentation and quantification.

Both evaluate DUX4 developmental repression (C99-C103 in OpenEval; C100-C113 in peer review). OpenEval finds the lack of early upregulation SUPPORTED, noting appropriate qualification of findings. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, finding the FSHD section 'overly technical' and requesting clearer presentation of significance, though not directly challenging the methylation data or contradiction with prior studies.

Peer reviewers rate the broader FSHD section UNCERTAIN due to difficulty understanding significance, though they don't specifically challenge the methylation methodology or 4qA-specific primer approach.

Peer reviewers rate the broader FSHD section UNCERTAIN but don't specifically challenge this control experiment, which strengthens the conclusion about 4qA allele behavior.

Both address 5-AzaC treatment effects (C112-C113). OpenEval finds dose-dependent DUX4 upregulation SUPPORTED, noting the regulatory locus is not identified. Peer reviewers rate the broader FSHD section UNCERTAIN, requesting clearer presentation of advances in FSHD modeling, though not directly challenging the 5-AzaC data.

Both evaluate xenograft engraftment (C114-C123 in OpenEval; C5-C7, C114-C128 in peer review). OpenEval finds immunofluorescence and qPCR data SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 requesting 'quantification of LAMIN A/C & SPECTRIN double positive donor derived fibers.' Agreement on successful engraftment but disagreement on sufficiency of quantification.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting more rigorous quantification of donor-derived fibers. Disagreement on whether RNA-based quantification is sufficient versus protein-based fiber counting.

Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 noting xenograft properties validate the lineage and Reviewer 2 not challenging the quantitative findings. Agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating 'LGMDR7: this section appears out of context and brief.' Disagreement on sufficiency of presentation and contextual integration.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'novelty is limited' and 'reported findings are very limited in terms of disease modelling,' citing prior work. Disagreement on novelty and significance rather than data quality.

Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting 'serial injuries or transplantation' validation, 'quantification of contribution to satellite cell pool,' and 'quantification of donor derived Pax7+ cells in vivo.'
